newsitem.title: USA: Pechiney cut still leaves U.S. bevcan overcapacity.
newsitem.headline: Pechiney cut still leaves U.S. bevcan overcapacity.

text.p: There is still overcapacity in the U.S. aluminum beverage can sector despite cutbacks announced by Pechiney SA at its American National Can operations, industry analysts said.
Pechiney said last week it planned to shut three billion cans of production capacity in the U.S. by the year-end, reducing capacity to 26-27 billion cans a year.

Pechiney's chairman and ceo, Jean Pierre Rodier told reporters in London earlier Monday that Pechiney will close two to three canmaking plants at undisclosed locations in the U.S. to reduce total capacity by 10 percent.
"This (intended closures) will improve the utilisation rate at the other facilities," Rodier said.
U.S. aluminum beverage can consumption in 1996 was just over 99 billion cans.
With about one pound of aluminum producing some 27 beverage cans, the reduction is equivalent to 50,400 tonnes a aluminum sheet a year in potential demand or the output of a small-sized rolling mill.
Although Pechiney is a major aluminum producer, its smelters are in Europe and ANC buys canstock from North American mills.
Robert Unger of Planned Technology Associates said despite the loss in capacity, ANC may well receive a boost from the new contoured can it is making in small lots for Coca-Cola.

ANC's contoured or bottle shaped can is being trialed by Coke-Cola this month in five U.S. markets, part of a three-year old initiative to promote the contour shape popularized generations ago by the glass Coke bottle.
There has been overcapacity in the U.S. canmaking industry for some time, market observers said.

Fred Church, editor of CanTech International journal, said some "buffer" excess capacity is needed to cope with surges in can demand during very hot weather, but the Pechiney cut will still not be enough to wipe out above normal surplus capacity.
"There will still be overcapacity in the U.S., but I don't consider it a threat for the industry," Church added.
A U.S. canstock producer official agreed: "I think there is some excess beverage can capacity in the U.S., but not to the extent it was in the past. It's pretty much in balance."

Nevertheless, with the PET plastic packaging becoming aggressive in the soft drinks sector, and can plants becoming more efficient, overcapacity may continue to be a problem for some time, Church said.
"I would think that ANC has the largest amount of overcapacity," Church said.
